title: What the homepage has to prove for a community sports club
metaTitle: What a club homepage has to prove
excerpt: A club homepage should show people playing, how to start, and a way to membership or the schedule. A trophy wall reassures the committee and stalls a new member.
alt: Two people pointing at a laptop screen, one wearing a fitness band. The shared screen is the decision a club homepage has to support.
caption: Two people point at a laptop together, one wearing a fitness band. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs on the first screen of a club homepage?
faqs.answer: Show people playing, one plain sentence on how a new person starts, and a single way to see membership or the schedule. Those three things let a stranger decide whether this is their weeknight. History, sponsors, and silverware can sit further down, or on a later page.

faqs.question: Why is a trophy wall a weak lead for a new member?
faqs.answer: Trophies reassure people who were already there. A person deciding whether to join reads a wall of cups as a closed group. Keep one season photograph on a review page if pride needs a home, and let the homepage be the door.

faqs.question: Does the homepage need the full timetable?
faqs.answer: It needs a true path to the timetable or to membership, in words the club already says out loud. Printing every slot is optional. Publishing a table that went stale in March is worse than a short link to the live board.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A community sports club homepage has one job for a person who might join. Show people playing, show how to start, and put membership or the schedule one clear step away. A wall of trophies fails that person. They already believe clubs own cups. They do not yet believe this is the room where their Tuesday goes.

The page is a decision. If the first screen cannot answer whether people like them play here, and what they should do next, the rest of the site is a brochure they will leave closed.

## The person on the page is choosing a weeknight

Someone looking for a club is choosing between staying home, a casual game in the park, and a membership they have not seen. They want the sport to look real, the room to look enterable, and the next step to be obvious. The committee's pride is a later concern.

Write in the order they ask. Who plays. How a new person starts. Where the times and the cost live. History, sponsors, and silverware wait until those three are settled. A founder briefing a studio, or a secretary briefing themselves, should be able to say that order out loud before anyone opens a layout.

Nielsen Norman Group's write-up on [how long people stay on web pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is blunt about the opening. Users often leave in 10 to 20 seconds. To earn several minutes of attention, the page has to communicate its value within about 10 seconds. The average visit lasts a little less than a minute, and people have time to read only about a quarter of the text on the pages they do visit. A homepage that opens on a founding year spends the only seconds that matter on a fact that does not change the decision.

That research also describes why the first moments feel harsh. People have met too many pages that waste them. They triage fast. If the club looks like every other club's noticeboard, they leave to try the next result, or they go back to the group chat that sent them.

## People playing, then how to start

The first photograph should be people in the activity, at a scale where a stranger can name the sport. Faces help. The ball, the mat, the ring, the boat, or the court helps more. A crop so tight that the picture becomes a texture fails the job. A posed lineup in matching hoodies, holding a cup, also fails it. That frame proves a photo day. It does not prove a session a new person can enter.

Put the photograph where the eye lands, and write how to start beside it, or directly under it on a phone. Beginners are welcome on Thursdays. The first session is a trial. Arrive twenty minutes early if you have never played. Bring indoor shoes. The sentence should sound like a coach at the door. If you cannot say it that plainly, the page is still performing for people who already belong.

Say who the session is for when that changes the choice. A social hit of badminton is a different promise from a junior academy with a waiting list. A masters crew that trains at dawn is a different promise from a learn-to-row course in September. Hide that distinction and you attract the wrong person, then spend the next month explaining the mismatch in person. The homepage can prevent that conversation.

Ballarat Box Sports is a public Hanabi project in this category: a community sports brand site. The useful lesson is the category. A club can have a point of view and a site that feels like the room, with the activity visible, without turning the homepage into a hall of fame. Treat it as an example of the kind of work. It is a reference for tone, and it is a finished public site you can look at. Specific results from that project stay off this page, because they were never published as a claim.

## Membership or the schedule, one step away

The person who believes the session is real will ask when it runs and what it costs. The homepage does not have to print every slot. It does have to offer a way to see membership or the schedule without a hunt through menus.

Name the link in words the club already says. Membership. This week's schedule. Train with us. Book a trial. Pick one. A button that says Explore, Learn more, or Join the family sends them into a maze. They arrived with a specific question. Answer it with a specific door.

If the schedule changes weekly, say where the live version lives and who updates it. A table that was true in March is worse than a short note that points at the current board. Trust breaks on a wrong kickoff time faster than it breaks on a plain typeface. If membership opens and closes with the season, say that in the same breath as the link. "Registration opens 1 September" is a useful sentence. "Be part of something bigger" is a stall.

Put the same path in the header. The first screen and the navigation should agree. A hero that offers the schedule, and a menu that buries it under Club, is two sites arguing. People on a phone will trust the thing they can tap without scrolling. Make that thing the real next step.

## A trophy case answers the wrong person

Trophies reassure the people who already belong. They record past seasons, and past seasons matter to members who were there. A new person reads a wall of cups as a closed group. The club looks successful and hard to enter. Success is attractive only after the door is visible.

If silverware belongs on the site at all, it belongs after the offer. A short line on a season page, or one photograph in a review of the year, can carry pride without blocking the entrance. The homepage is the entrance. Sponsors follow the same rule. A logo grid can sit low on the page if those partners paid for a mention. It should never be the picture that explains the club.

The same miss shows up in other costumes. A quote from the president about values, with no picture of play. A video that opens on a drone shot of the building. A slider of three slogans. Each one answers a question the visitor has not asked yet. Google's notes on [people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) ask whether a page has a real audience who would find it useful if they came to you directly, and whether they leave able to do the thing they came to do. A committee filling the homepage with awards is writing for the committee. The person who might join leaves to look somewhere else.

## What the first screen actually holds

Keep the first view small enough to read in those opening seconds. Four things are enough.

- The sport, in a picture of people playing.
- One sentence on who it is for, including beginners when that is true.
- How to start, in the coach's words.
- One way to see membership or the schedule.

Everything else is a later section. Coming fixtures. A map. A note on kit. Age bands, if age bands matter. The committee, if someone asks for names. Do not stack them above the decision. A long hero that requires scrolling before the link appears has spent the 10 seconds on atmosphere.

Type should be ordinary and large enough on a phone. The club's name can be quiet. The activity should be loud. A clever line that only current members understand is an in-joke at the door. Save the in-joke for the notice that members see after they join.

If you design the wide layout first, look at the phone before you approve it. The picture, the sentence, and the link have to survive a narrow screen. A crop of someone's shoulder, with the button below the first view, is a different homepage. Design the narrow screen as the real one, then let the wide screen have more of the same picture.

## The rest of the page follows the same order

Below the first screen, repeat the sequence in longer form. A strip of ordinary sessions, with captions that say what is happening. A plain account of the first visit: where to stand, who to find, what the first half hour feels like. Then the facts. The hall or the ground. The general pattern of the week. What to bring. Who to ask if you are bringing a child.

A map matters when the entrance is on the side street. Parking and the door to use matter more than a history of the building. Kit matters when the wrong shoes will stop someone playing. Say it in a sentence each. A paragraph of atmosphere around each fact makes the fact harder to find, and people are already reading only a fraction of what you wrote.

Ages and ability need their own clear lines when the club runs more than one kind of session. Juniors at 5. Seniors at 7. A supervised trial before anyone is placed in a squad. Safeguarding is part of the offer for a parent, so the page should say that a junior session is coached and supervised, in plain language, without turning the homepage into a policy PDF. Link the policy. Do not paste it over the picture of children playing. Get consent for any photograph of minors before it goes near the site. That is a production rule, not a caption style.

Sponsors, history, and life members can have a modest place once the offer is clear. End the page by repeating the path. The person who scrolled is more convinced, and still needs a next step. Membership or the schedule, again, in the same words as the top.

## What to bring to the brief

If you hand this page to a studio, bring three things. Recent photographs of ordinary sessions, with permission from the people in them. The true first-visit rules, including anything that would surprise a beginner. The place where membership and the schedule actually live, even if that place is a messy document today.

You do not need a brand manual the size of a league handbook. You need the order, and you need someone who will protect it when a well-meaning volunteer asks for a slider of last year's final. Hanabi designs and builds sites in that spirit: the first screen does a job, and the rest of the page supports it. The public sports example is there to look at, not to copy line for line.

Once the homepage shows play and a way in, the next question is what joining costs and what the fee covers. That decision sits on [a pricing page for a community sports club](/blog/a-pricing-page-for-a-community-sports-club).

Community and sports sites with a visible activity live among [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). Look for whether the first screen shows people doing the thing, and a way to take the next step.
